In 2026, Google AI Studio’s **Build Mode** (and its cousin, **Firebase Studio**) has become remarkably sophisticated at "vibe coding" full-stack apps.

To get a functional logistics tracker, you need a prompt that covers three things: **Role-based access** (Merchant vs. Driver), **Real-time Map tracking**, and **Data persistence** (so your information doesn't vanish).

### The "Master Prompt" for Google AI Studio

Copy and paste this into the **Build** tab in Google AI Studio:

> **Act as a Senior Full-Stack Developer. Build a logistics tracking web application using React and Tailwind CSS.**
> **Core Functionality:**
> 1. **Authentication:** Create a login page with two roles: "Merchant" and "Driver".
> 2. **Merchant Dashboard:** >    * Display a full-screen **Google Maps view**.
> * Show real-time markers (truck icons) for all active drivers.
> * When a marker is clicked, show a side panel with the driver's name and a "Cargo Manifest" (List of items, quantities, and destination).
> 
> 
> 3. **Driver Interface:** >    * A mobile-optimized screen with a large "Start Trip / Stop Trip" toggle.
> * When "Start Trip" is active, use the browser's Geolocation API to send live coordinates to the database every 10 seconds.
> * A form to "Log Cargo" where they can input what they are carrying.
> 
> 
> 4. **Real-time Data:** Use **Firebase Firestore** as the backend to sync driver coordinates and cargo logs instantly between the Driver app and the Merchant map.
> 5. **Design:** Modern, clean "Logistics Tech" aesthetic. Use a dark sidebar for the Merchant and large, accessible buttons for the Driver.
> 
> 
> **Grounding:** Please use the Google Maps JavaScript API for the mapping features and ensure the code includes placeholders for my Firebase and Google Maps API keys.

---

### Pro-Tips for the Best Result:

* **Select the right model:** In the top right of AI Studio, ensure you are using **Gemini 3 Pro** or **Gemini 2.5 Pro** (which is specifically optimized for Google Maps grounding).
* **Iterate after the first build:** Once the app appears in the preview pane, you can "talk" to it to fix things. For example: *"The driver buttons are too small for someone wearing gloves; make them bigger and bright green."*
* **Deployment:** When you're happy, look for the **"Deploy to Cloud Run"** button in AI Studio. It will give you a live link you can actually open on your phone and a merchant's laptop.

### A Quick Recommendation

Since you’re a student at UWI, you might have access to Google Cloud credits through your university email. If so, I’d recommend using **Firebase Studio** (at `firebase.studio`) with this same prompt. It’s slightly more "hands-off" for the database setup than the standard AI Studio.

**Addressing Key Restrictions**

I've hit a snag regarding real Firebase and Google Maps integration, as direct API key usage isn't feasible. I'm now crafting a "Service Layer" that defaults to mock data if API keys are absent, while supporting actual integration when keys are provided. I'm leaning toward employing a `store.ts` (using React Context or a simple state manager) to mimic Firebase with `localStorage`.


**Refining the Simulation**

I'm now prioritizing a robust "Local Simulation" that mirrors the functionality of a real Firebase backend. I am using `setInterval` to create the demo for the user. I'll structure the code (using React state for the immediate demo) exactly as one would hook up Firebase, with hooks for data fetching. This way, real Firebase can be readily integrated. I'll add clarifying comments on Firebase SDK initialization.


**Outlining The Structure**

I'm now focusing on setting up the fundamental structure. I'm working with the React Root in `index.tsx` and main routing in `App.tsx`. I've defined types for Driver, Cargo, and UserRole in `types.ts`. I'm breaking down the components into Auth, MerchantDashboard, DriverDashboard, and Map. I'm setting up a mock backend in `mockBackend.ts` to interact immediately, and am going to setup all of the initial mock implementation.


**Implementing the Map**

I'm now implementing the Google Maps component within the Merchant UI. I'm building it around a sidebar layout. I'll integrate the Google Maps script dynamically using `useEffect` in `App.tsx` and have a fallback for API key issues. Driver logic will use `navigator.geolocation.watchPosition`, and the map logic utilizes `new google.maps.Map(...)` for markers and other Google Maps API elements.


**Defining the Details**

I'm now detailing the application's visual style and addressing prompt specifics. I'm focusing on Tailwind color palettes and standard sans fonts to establish the visual "vibe". I'm addressing the prompt requirements, particularly the "real-time markers" and the use of the Google Maps API. My implementation involves several XML files, and I'm beginning the XML content. I'm meticulously designing the `services/firebaseConfig.ts` to simulate Firestore subscriptions for UI realism, even without a key, particularly for "Show me the code" requests. I'll separate the View from the rest.


**Simulating the Data**

I'm now focused on implementing a React Context, `LogisticsContext`, to manage the state and simulate real-time updates between the Driver and Merchant components. This mimics the Firestore snapshot listener behavior, ensuring the Merchant's view immediately reflects driver actions. Additionally, I am now focused on a map simulation to substitute for the Google Map component, if the API key is not present. I'll make the map code "real" but robust.
